scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4673: It's the IT department office here (our machines are
the 192.168.1.x ones). None of our computers can get to anything on the
network any more -- not the shared drives, not the other departments,
nothing, and it hit all of us at the same time. A whole room does not go
dark together on its own. Someone here said it plainly: the department
switch has died. I wouldn't know which box that is or where it lives, but it
is your box and your job to find it. Check whatever connects our room to the
rest of the campus and get us back on today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The IT-segment switch is passing traffic: IT
  hosts (it_hod, it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach
  each other on 192.168.1.0/24. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of an L2 switch failure that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the IT-dept switch (switch0)
failed and took down the IT segment -- is NOT reproducible: IT hosts (it_hod,
it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach each other across
192.168.1.0/24, which means the L2 switch is passing traffic normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the IT-segment switch is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces IT host -> gateway and
host -> host pings, finds them all 0% loss (proving L2 connectivity through the
switch), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a failed switch -- declaring the
IT segment down to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
No network fault is present. The IT department (192.168.1.0/24) has full,
end-to-end connectivity to every other segment in the topology. A thorough
inspection of all relevant components found no anomaly at any layer.

At Layer 2, switch0 — the device connecting the IT LAN (eth1, lan_it) to
router0 (eth0, link_r0_sw0) — is completely healthy. Its Linux bridge br0
has both ports in STP forwarding state with no errors or dropped frames.

At Layer 3, router0 has all three interfaces up (192.168.1.1/24 facing IT,
192.168.2.1/24 facing CS, 10.10.0.1/8 WAN to router1) and its RIP routing
table carries correct learned routes to every remote subnet (192.168.3–4.x,
1.0.0.0/8, 20.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16). Router1 and router2 likewise carry
reciprocal routes back to 192.168.1.0/24. No iptables rules exist anywhere
in the forwarding path.

Live ping tests from five IT hosts (it_hod, it_lab1, it_lab2, it_lab3,
it_lab4) to targets in the office, CS, server, internet, and principal
segments all completed with 0% packet loss.

Root cause: There is no fault. The reported outage is not substantiated by
any current state in the lab.

Corrective action: No configuration change is required. The helpdesk ticket
should be closed as a false report; on-site staff should verify whether the
issue was transient (a brief cable pull, a device that needed rebooting) and
has already self-resolved, or whether the report was filed in error.

per_axis.rationale: The writeup does not explicitly state IT hosts pinged their gateway 192.168.1.1 and each other on 192.168.1.0/24 with 0% loss — it only mentions broad 0% loss to other segments.

The investigation log contains multiple successful ping outputs between IT hosts and routers/remote hosts, an it_hod route showing default gateway 192.168.1.1, bridge STP output for br0, and iptables showing no filtering — so the writeup's claims are grounded and the conclusion (no fault) follows logically.
